paper.title: Debt/Equity Ratio and Expected Common Stock Returns: Empirical Evidence
paper.citation: Bhandari, Laxmi Chand (1988), The Journal of Finance, 43(2), 507-528.

definition.value: Debt/equity ratio (DER), defined as the book value of total assets minus the book value of common equity, divided by the market value of common equity, measured at accounting year-ends.

evidence.location: Section I, Model, Data, and Test Design
evidence.quote: DER is the ratio: book value of total assets - book value of common equity / market value of common equity measured at the accounting year-ends.

economic_intuition.value: Higher debt/equity increases the risk of common equity and is expected to be positively correlated with expected common stock returns when other explanatory variables do not adequately control for risk.

evidence.location: Introduction
evidence.quote: An increase in the DER of a firm increases the risk of its common equity, measuring risk in any reasonable way.

evidence.location: Introduction
evidence.quote: With risk-averse investors, we expect a positive correlation between DER and the expected common stock returns when the other explanatory variables used are inadequate to control for risk.

evidence.location: Section III, Summary and Conclusions
evidence.quote: The expected returns on common stocks are positively related to the debt/equity ratio (DER), controlling for the beta and firm size, both including and excluding January.

notes: This paper's target is the monthly Fama-MacBeth expected-return regression coefficient on DER, conditional on LTEQ and BETA, rather than a conventional long-short factor return. The paper uses sequential 3-by-3-by-3 portfolio formation to create 27 portfolios before estimating monthly cross-sectional regressions.
